clue.text: Dispute in members' lobby

parts.note: a lobby is an entrance hall or corridor, a passage
members are limbs such as arms, so the possessive 'members'' reads as 'of arms'

explanation.surface: MPs are arguing in the lobby of the House where members gather.
explanation.walkthrough: The parliamentary picture of 'members' lobby' hides limbs: arms are members of the body, and a lobby is a passage, so 'members' lobby' becomes a passage of arms.
explanation.definitionFit: A passage of arms is an old phrase for a fight or a heated exchange of words, a quarrel.

clue.text: Emerges from grand anteroom slowly

indicators.note: Emerges from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone comes slowly out of a large waiting room.
explanation.definitionFit: Andante is the musical tempo marking for a moderately slow, walking pace.

clue.text: Sx machine-gun

parts.note: the picture shows the letter S followed by x, the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.walkthrough: Read the picture 'Sx' as S and then x, which in Roman numerals is ten, so it says S followed by the number ten.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sten was a cheap British submachine gun of the Second World War.

clue.text: If you do, chill out!

parts.note: advice that reads as 'relax' but literally says that becoming chilly will leave you chilled

explanation.surface: Someone is told that if they act, they should calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chill out' looks like slang for relax; read literally, catching a chill is what happens when you lose warmth.
explanation.definitionFit: To grow chilly is to become cold, which is literally being chilled.

clue.text: Died with few debts, as is evident

parts.note: OB, short for Latin obiit, is the abbreviation for died
V is the Roman numeral for five, the number the setter must have meant
IOUs are written promises to pay, so they are debts

explanation.surface: A man passed away owing very little, as everyone could see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Died' is the abbreviation from Latin obiit. The answer needs the Roman five after it; 'few' cannot give that, so the clue as held seems to have lost the word 'five'. 'as is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obvious is plain to see, clear and apparent.

clue.text: Isn't vulgar

parts.note: reads as a judgement that something is in good taste, but asks for the slang, non-standard form of 'isn't'

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a verdict that something is tasteful; instead 'vulgar' means common speech, and the clue asks for the colloquial contraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Ain't is a colloquial, non-standard contraction used in place of is not or are not.

clue.text: Manipulate idiot taken in by sorcerer

indicators.note: taken in by says the word for idiot sits inside the word for sorcerer

parts.note: a mage is a magician or sorcerer
an ass is a fool or idiot

explanation.surface: A gullible fool is duped by a wizard into doing his bidding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' suggests being duped, which suits the surface, but here it is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To massage is to knead the body with the hands, and also to manipulate figures dishonestly.

clue.text: Barrister made irate collier hold hatchet up

parts.note: someone made irate is angry, or cross

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word for hatchet is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a hatchet is a small axe
a collier is a coal miner

explanation.surface: A lawyer has angered a coal miner by making him raise an axe.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' turns the hatchet so it reads from the bottom; 'hold' is only a link here, and 'made irate' is the adjective cross, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrister in court questions the other side's witnesses, cross-examining them.

clue.text: Headhunter reads stories about biblical clay-worker

indicators.note: about says the word for stories goes round the biblical abbreviation

parts.note: tales are stories
NT, the New Testament, is a biblical abbreviation
a potter shapes clay into pots

explanation.surface: A recruiter reads tales about a potter from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'biblical' gives the abbreviation for the New Testament; 'reads' is only a link. The potter of Jeremiah's parable shapes clay.
explanation.definitionFit: A headhunter in business recruits gifted staff, someone who finds promising performers.

clue.text: Yeomen's preferred fare?

parts.note: the Yeomen Warders of the Tower of London are nicknamed Beefeaters, so their favourite food is beef

explanation.walkthrough: The Yeomen Warders who guard the Tower of London are popularly called Beefeaters; beef is the classic dark meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef, lamb and similar dark meats are called red meat, the food a beef-eater would choose.

clue.text: She takes weathercocks to south Africa

parts.note: weathercocks are weather vanes

explanation.surface: A woman carries weather vanes off to South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Vanessa is a girl's name, so a woman can be referred to by it.

clue.text: "Peccavi — I have - - ." (sir Charles Napier)

parts.note: Napier's reported one-word dispatch after conquering the province was Latin for 'I have sinned', a pun on the province's name

explanation.walkthrough: General Sir Charles Napier is said to have reported his 1843 conquest of the Indian province with the Latin 'Peccavi', meaning 'I have sinned', which sounds like the place he took.
explanation.definitionFit: Sind, now Sindh in Pakistan, was the province Napier captured, its name sounding like a word for having done wrong.

clue.text: Choose to attack

explanation.definitionFit: To go for something is to select it; to go for someone is to set upon them.

clue.text: People in competition

explanation.definitionFit: A race is a group of people of common descent; it is also a contest of speed.

clue.text: Many a refuse-collector on board ship

parts.note: C, the Roman numeral for a hundred, stands for many
a bin collects refuse

explanation.surface: A host of dustmen are on board a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' is C, the Roman hundred. The definition describes the answer rather than naming it: a sleeping room you find on board ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabin is a private room for passengers or crew aboard a vessel.

clue.text: Unnerve American spy

explanation.definitionFit: To spook is to frighten someone; spook is also US slang for a secret agent.

clue.text: Beryl, perhaps, brought me back real cut diamonds

indicators.note: back says the word me is turned round to read in reverse

parts.note: taken as written before it is turned

indicators.note: cut means the letters of real are chopped up and rearranged

parts.note: D is the card abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: A woman's gift of cut diamonds brought her back to the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns ME into EM, and 'cut' turns REAL into ERAL. 'Beryl, perhaps' looks like a woman's name but is the mineral.
explanation.definitionFit: The emerald is the green gem variety of the mineral beryl, so beryl may be one.

clue.text: Wise enough to repair panties

indicators.note: to repair is to mend by putting pieces back in a new order, so the letters of panties are reworked

explanation.surface: Someone is clever enough to mend their own underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enough to' is a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapient is a formal word for wise or sagacious.

clue.text: Used when a couple of coppers falsified facts

parts.note: a copper is a penny, P, so two of them give PP
someone who falsified facts lied

explanation.surface: It was put into practice when two police officers lied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' are police in the surface, but here they are copper coins, pennies, each abbreviated P.
explanation.definitionFit: Something applied has been put to use or brought into practice.

clue.text: Left one business in the arcade

parts.note: port is the left-hand side of a ship
I is the Roman numeral one
CO is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: Someone left a single shop in the shopping arcade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the' is a link. An arcade here is a row of columns, not a shopping street.
explanation.definitionFit: A portico is a covered porch of columns, a form of colonnade or arcade.

clue.text: "A - - horrible, on all sides round as one great furnace flam'd;" Milton's paradise lost

definitions.text: "A - - horrible, on all sides round as one great furnace flam'd;" Milton's paradise lost

parts.words: "A - - horrible, on all sides round as one great furnace flam'd;" Milton's paradise lost
parts.note: the missing word completes Milton's description of Hell in Book I of the epic poem

explanation.walkthrough: In Book I of Paradise Lost, Milton describes Hell as a horrible prison flaming like a furnace; the gap is that prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A dungeon is an underground prison cell, Milton's image for the pit of Hell.

clue.text: Temporary expedient to plug dental cavity

parts.note: to plug a hole is to stop it
a gap is a space, as between teeth

explanation.surface: A dentist uses a short-term fix to fill a hole in a tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopgap is a makeshift measure used until something better is found.

clue.text: Resin the man will put into bag

indicators.note: put into says the words for the man will go inside the word for bag

parts.note: a sac is a bag or pouch
he'll is the contraction for he will, the man will

explanation.surface: A man will pack some resin into a bag.
explanation.definitionFit: Shellac is a resin secreted by the lac insect, used in varnish.

clue.text: Refuse to leave hold-all in Parisian station

indicators.note: in says the word for hold-all sits inside the French word for station

parts.note: gare is French for station, as found in Paris
a hold-all is a bag

explanation.surface: Someone declines to abandon a travel bag at a Paris railway terminus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb, but it is the noun meaning rubbish; 'to leave' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Garbage is rubbish, household waste.

clue.text: Oriental pill-box found in Romania

indicators.note: found says the answer is a run of letters lying inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: An eastern box for pills is discovered in Romania.
explanation.definitionFit: An inro is a small Japanese case worn at the sash to hold medicines and seals.

clue.text: Finger a directory

explanation.definitionFit: The index is the forefinger; an index is also an alphabetical list or directory.

clue.text: Courage? The last king had it

parts.note: GR, George Rex, was the cipher of the last British king, George VI

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the late king had bravery.
explanation.walkthrough: GR stands for Georgius Rex; the last British king was George VI. 'had' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Grit is resolve and determination, a kind of bravery.

clue.text: Part of the addition, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says a word that is spoken is to be replaced by one sounding the same

parts.note: the result of an addition is the sum

explanation.surface: A piece of the total is overheard.
explanation.definitionFit: Some means a portion or quantity of something.

clue.text: Expert goes into action erecting grandstands

indicators.note: goes into says the answer lies inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A specialist gets busy putting up stands at a stadium.
explanation.definitionFit: A oner is an informal British word for someone outstanding at something, an ace.

clue.text: Perfect example of exotic pie in my view

indicators.note: exotic means strange or foreign, so the letters of pie appear in an unfamiliar order

parts.note: in my view is the same as to me

explanation.surface: An unusual pie is, in the speaker's opinion, the model of its kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exotic' turns PIE into EPI; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitome is a typical, ideal instance that sums up a whole class.

clue.text: Rule a long time, despite strain

parts.note: to rule is to draw a line
an age is a long time

explanation.surface: Someone reigns for many years despite pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rule' looks like reigning, but it is ruling a line; 'despite' is a link. 'strain' looks like stress but is ancestry.
explanation.definitionFit: A strain is a line of descent or ancestry, as is a lineage.

clue.text: Eccentric loner anchored in secret

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the letters of loner anchored are rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd recluse has dropped anchor out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Hole-and-corner describes something done furtively and underhand.
